extracted.intended_audience: conference program committees, peer-review researchers, and conference organizers interested in reviewing policy
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of single-blind versus double-blind conference reviewing using a controlled experiment at WSDM 2017 to measure bidding behaviour and acceptance recommendation biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer identity visibility (single-blind vs double-blind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-blind reviewing: committee members are aware of the names and affiliations of paper authors. Double-blind reviewing: this information is not visible to committee members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary experimental condition contrasted in the study; visibility of author identity is treated as a factor that can induce bias at bidding and recommendation stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled experimental design with split reviewer pools
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paper was reviewed by four committee members. Two of these four reviewers were chosen from a pool of committee members who had access to author information; the other two were chosen from a disjoint pool who did not have access to this information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design note / standard for validity: use disjoint reviewer pools and assign multiple reviewers per paper across conditions to isolate the effect of identity visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of information asymmetry through workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: The information asymmetry (whether a reviewer could see author identities) persisted through the process of bidding for papers, reviewing papers, and entering scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating reviewing regimes, track whether identity visibility is maintained only at review time or also during bidding and scoring, since effects can arise at any stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidding rate (reviewer engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-blind reviewers typically bid for 22% fewer papers than double-blind reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bid counts or relative change (e.g., percent fewer bids) as a metric of how identity visibility affects reviewer willingness to bid; low bid rates may affect reviewer-paper matching quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferential bidding for papers from top institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-blind reviewers preferentially bid for papers from top institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure distribution of bids by author affiliation rank/status to detect selection bias at the bidding stage; compare across blind conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance recommendation bias for famous authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-blind reviewers were significantly more likely than double-blind reviewers to recommend for acceptance papers from famous authors; estimated odds multiplier = 1.63 for famous authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify author-name fame effect using odds ratios and statistical tests; include confidence intervals and significance tests when reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance recommendation bias for top universities and companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-blind reviewers were significantly more likely than double-blind reviewers to recommend for acceptance papers from top universities and from top companies; estimated odds multipliers = 1.58 (top universities) and 2.10 (top companies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report separate institution-type effects (e.g., universities vs companies) and provide odds multipliers to convey effect size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender effect on acceptance recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: For female authors, the associated odds multiplier of acceptance recommendation in this study is 0.78 (not statistically significant in this single study), though a meta-analysis places this value in line with other experiments and in aggregate the gender effect is statistically significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate gender effects both within the single experiment (report odds multipliers and significance) and in meta-analytic context; be explicit about statistical power and aggregation across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of odds multipliers and statistical significance / meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The study reports estimated odds multipliers for effects (e.g., fame, institution, gender) and references meta-analysis to assess aggregate significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing bias effects, report effect-size metrics (odds ratios/multipliers), statistical significance, and where appropriate place single-study estimates in the context of meta-analytic evidence to judge robustness.
